title: The future

objectives.can: Recognise and parse future indicative forms, active, middle and passive.

explanation.summary: The Greek future is built on its own stem, usually the verb's stem with a σ added. It has the present's endings, no augment, and three groups of forms: active, middle and passive. This lesson shows how the future is made and how to find the headword behind it.

sections.heading: What the future does
body: In the indicative the future usually places an action after the time of speaking: 'he will give', 'you will see'. It is also used in other ways. In quotations from the Law, the future often states a command, as in 'you shall love'.

The future exists in the indicative, and also in the participle and the infinitive, which you will learn later. There is no future subjunctive and no future imperative. The future indicative has no augment, because the augment marks past time.

sections.heading: Making the future: stem, σ and endings
body: The regular future adds σ to the verb stem and then uses the present endings: -ω, -εις, -ει, -ομεν, -ετε, -ουσι(ν) in the active, and -ομαι, -ῃ, -εται, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -ονται in the middle. The σ before the connecting vowel is the sign of the future, as in πιστεύσει from πιστεύω and ἀκούσουσιν from ἀκούω.

A stem ending in a vowel simply takes σ. If the stem ends in a short vowel, the vowel is usually lengthened: contract verbs usually lengthen ε to η, α to η and ο to ω, so that ποιέω gives ποιήσει, ἀγαπάω gives ἀγαπήσεις and ἐρωτάω gives ἐρωτήσω. A few keep the short vowel, such as καλέω, which has καλέσεις.

sections.heading: When the stem ends in a consonant
body: When a consonant stem meets σ, the two combine. A stem ending in π, β or φ and σ make ψ; a stem ending in κ, γ or χ and σ make ξ; a stem ending in τ, δ, θ or ζ simply loses that letter before σ. You can recognise a future ψ- or ξ-form by looking back from the ψ or ξ to the present stem.
The table gives an example of each pattern from the texts.

sections.heading: Liquid verbs
body: A verb whose stem ends in λ, μ, ν or ρ, a liquid, has no σ in the future. Instead it has an ε that contracts with the ending, so that the future endings are those of a contract verb in -έω: -ῶ, -εῖς, -εῖ, -οῦμεν, -εῖτε, -οῦσι(ν). Examples are ἀποστέλλω, whose future is ἀποστελεῖ; κρίνω, with κρινεῖ; and ἀποκτείνω, with ἀποκτενοῦσιν.

A liquid future can look like a present form, and sometimes the only difference is the accent: κρίνει is present and κρινεῖ is future. Context and accent decide. The present of ἀποστέλλω is ἀποστέλλει, with double λ; the future has only one λ and a circumflex.

sections.heading: Futures that are middle in form
body: A number of common verbs have a future with middle endings and an active sense, in the way ἔρχομαι is middle in form in the present. The future of εἰμί is ἔσομαι, ἔσται, ἔσονται. Others are ὄψομαι (from ὁράω, 'I see'), γνώσομαι (from γινώσκω), ἐλεύσομαι (from ἔρχομαι), and καυχήσομαι (from καυχάομαι). λήμψεσθε, from λαμβάνω, is another.
Some of these futures come from a different stem than the present: ὁράω gives ὄψομαι, and ἔρχομαι gives ἐλεύσομαι. Learn them as they come; a lexicon will list them under the present.

sections.heading: The future passive
body: The future passive has -θησ- before the middle-and-passive endings: σωθήσεται, δοθήσεται, ἐγερθήσεται, κληθήσεται. The sequence -θησ- is the mark of the passive future. The endings are the usual -ομαι, -ῃ, -εται, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -ονται, and the sense is 'will be saved', 'will be given', 'will be raised', 'will be called'.
A future passive can take an agent with ὑπό, just as a present passive does. It is more often used without one.

misunderstandings: The σ is not always visible. In a liquid future there is no σ at all, and in ψ and ξ it is hidden in the double consonant. Reading these forms backwards means taking the ending away and finding the present stem.

A form that looks like a future may be something else. ποιήσω can be a future indicative or an aorist subjunctive, and the same is true of other -σω forms. The surrounding words, such as ἵνα or ἐάν, usually show which. This lesson asks only about the indicative.
Middle endings in the future do not make a verb reflexive or passive. ὄψεσθε means 'you will see', and ἔσται means 'will be'.
-θησ- does not make a verb future by itself: it marks the passive of the future. The matching aorist passive is taught later.

deeper.heading: Futures from another stem
body: A few verbs take their future from a stem that is quite different from the present. λέγω has the future ἐρῶ, ἐρεῖς, ἐρεῖ, ἐροῦμεν, ἐρεῖτε, ἐροῦσιν, which are liquid-type forms from a different root. They are not a mistake or a separate verb, so a lexicon lists them under λέγω.

examples.analysis: πέμψει, διδάξει and ὑπομνήσει are all third person singular, future active indicative. πέμψει comes from πέμπω: π + σ gives ψ. διδάξει comes from διδάσκω: the stem consonant combines with σ to give ξ.
